name: Colosseum
summary: The largest amphitheatre of the Roman world, where around 50,000 spectators watched gladiators and wild-animal hunts. It later became a fortress, a quarry and a Christian shrine.

eras.label: 80 CE
eras.title: One hundred days of games
eras.text: Emperor Vespasian began the amphitheatre around 70–72 CE, on the site of a private lake in Nero's palace gardens. His son Titus opened it in 80 CE with 100 days of games. Entry was free. Seats were arranged by rank, with senators at the front and women and the poor at the top. The painting shown here is a 19th-century imagining of a fight.

image.alt: Jean-Léon Gérôme's 1872 painting of gladiators in the Colosseum

eras.label: c. 90 CE
eras.title: The world underground
eras.text: Emperor Domitian added the hypogeum, a maze of tunnels, cages and lifts beneath the arena floor. Animals and scenery could rise suddenly through trapdoors in front of the crowd. Today the floor is gone, and you can look straight down into this hidden world.

image.alt: The underground tunnels of the Colosseum

eras.title: Earthquake and quarry
eras.text: The last recorded games took place in the 6th century. Over the centuries the building housed workshops, homes and even a noble family's fortress. A great earthquake in 1349 brought down the outer wall on the south side. Its fallen stone was carted away to build palaces and churches across Rome.

image.file: Giovanni Battista Piranesi - Views of Rome- The Colosseum - 1922.225 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
image.alt: Piranesi's 18th-century etching of the ruined Colosseum

eras.title: A place of martyrs
eras.text: In 1749 Pope Benedict XIV declared the Colosseum a sacred place in memory of early Christian martyrs, and this finally stopped the stone robbing. Stations of the Cross were set up around the arena. Historians now doubt that many Christians actually died here.

image.file: Cole Thomas Interior of the Colosseum Rome 1832.jpg
image.alt: Thomas Cole's 1832 painting of the Colosseum interior with a cross

eras.label: c. 1850
eras.title: A garden of ruins
eras.text: In the 1800s, travellers on the Grand Tour came to see the Colosseum by moonlight. Brick buttresses were added to stop the broken walls collapsing. In 1855 a botanist counted more than 400 species of wild plants growing among the stones.

image.alt: Painting of the ruined Colosseum beside the Arch of Constantine

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Icon of Rome
eras.text: Cleaned in a restoration that ended in 2016, the travertine glows honey-coloured again. The Colosseum is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Rome's historic centre and is one of the most visited monuments in the world.

story.title: Bread and circuses
story.narration: The Roman poet Juvenal complained that the people wanted only two things: bread and circuses. Emperors gave both. A day at the Colosseum was free, a gift from the emperor that showed off his power and generosity. Spectators passed through numbered arches, still visible above the entrances today, to their places. On hot days, sailors from the Roman navy stretched huge canvas awnings over the seats to give shade. Morning shows featured exotic animals from across the empire, and gladiators fought in the afternoon.

story.title: While the Colosseum stands

image.file: Jodocus Sebastiaen van den Abeele - View of the Colosseum in Rome.jpg
image.alt: Painting of the Colosseum in Rome

story.narration: The Romans called it the Flavian Amphitheatre, after the family of emperors who built it. The name Colosseum probably came later, from the Colossus, a giant bronze statue of Nero that once stood nearby. In the Middle Ages, pilgrims repeated a prophecy linked to the English monk Bede. While the Colosseum stands, Rome shall stand. When the Colosseum falls, Rome shall fall. And when Rome falls, the world will fall with it. Battered by earthquakes and stone thieves, the building has never quite fallen.

story.title: The life of a gladiator

image.alt: Detail of Gérôme's painting Pollice Verso

story.narration: Most gladiators were slaves or prisoners of war, but some free men volunteered for the fame and the prize money. They trained in schools such as the Ludus Magnus, whose ruins you can still see beside the Colosseum. Gladiators were expensive to train, so not every fight ended in death. A defeated fighter could be spared if the crowd and the emperor wished it. The famous thumbs-down gesture comes largely from this 1872 painting by Jean-Léon Gérôme. What Roman crowds actually did with their thumbs is still debated.

story.title: From arena to symbol of life

image.file: Franz Ludwig Catel - Parti af Colosseum i måneskin.jpg
image.alt: Painting of the Colosseum by moonlight

story.narration: Today the Colosseum carries new meanings. Every Good Friday, the Pope leads the Way of the Cross here by torchlight, a tradition that draws crowds from around the world. And since the year 2000, the monument has been lit up in gold each time a country abolishes the death penalty. A place once famous for violent death now stands as a symbol for the value of human life.

guide.price: Timed tickets usually include the Roman Forum and Palatine Hill. Book online with your name, because tickets are personal and you may be asked for ID. The underground and arena floor need special tickets.

hours.notes: Approximate. Closing time follows sunset, and the last entry is one hour before closing. Closed on 25 December and 1 January.

do: Book a timed ticket online well in advance, especially in spring and summer.
Carry a refillable bottle and fill it at the free "nasoni" drinking fountains.
Wear comfortable shoes. The ancient stone is uneven and there are many stairs.
Cover your shoulders and knees if you plan to visit nearby churches.
dont: Carve or scratch anything on the walls. Tourists have been heavily fined for this.
Pay costumed "gladiators" for photos without agreeing a price first.
Bring large backpacks or suitcases. Security will turn them away.

tips.title: Eat in Monti
tips.text: Skip the tourist menus right by the monument and walk ten minutes to the Monti district for carbonara, cacio e pepe or supplì (fried rice balls).

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: Metro line B stops at Colosseo, directly opposite the monument. Tram 3 and several buses also stop nearby.

tips.title: Golden hour
tips.text: Late afternoon light turns the travertine gold. For the best photos of the outside, walk up to the Colle Oppio park or Via Nicola Salvi.
